title: Log-Log Linearization of Power Function Models
originalTopic: Function Modeling: Power Laws and Log-Log Regression
author: Muhammad Abdullah Athar
problemStatement: Given a power function model y = a*x^b (with a > 0, x > 0), show how taking logarithms linearizes the equation, and explain how the constants a and b are determined from the slope and intercept of the resulting line.
finalAnswer: \ln y = b \ln x + \ln a; \quad \text{Slope } m = b, \quad y\text{-intercept } B = \ln a \implies a = e^B

steps.title: Take the Natural Logarithm of Both Sides
steps.explanation: Apply the natural logarithm to both sides of the power function equation, which is valid for positive x and a.
steps.why: Logarithmic functions are strictly monotonic, preserving equivalence for positive arguments.

steps.title: Apply Logarithmic Product and Power Rules
steps.mathExpression: \ln(a x^b) = \ln a + \ln(x^b) = \ln a + b \ln x = b \ln x + \ln a
steps.explanation: Use ln(uv) = ln u + ln v and ln(u^b) = b ln u to separate constants and exponents into linear coefficients.
steps.why: Fundamental properties of logarithms convert multiplicative powers into additive linear products.

steps.title: Interpret in Linear Form Y = mX + B
steps.mathExpression: Y = m X + B \quad \text{where } Y = \ln y, \ X = \ln x, \ m = b, \ B = \ln a
steps.explanation: Plotting ln y against ln x yields a straight line where the slope m directly equals the power exponent b, and the vertical intercept B gives the scale factor a = e^B.
steps.why: Linear regression analysis on transformed coordinate variables determines power-law parameters.
